name: Seine (French: la Seine)
location_description: The Seine flows through northern France, rising in the Langres plateau at Source-Seine (Cote-d'Or department, Burgundy), about 30 km northwest of Dijon, and running generally northwest across the Paris Basin to its mouth on the English Channel between Le Havre and Honfleur in Normandy. It is the river that runs through Paris, the capital of France: over roughly 13 km within the city it divides Paris into the Left Bank (Rive Gauche) and Right Bank (Rive Droite), and its islands - the Ile de la Cite and Ile Saint-Louis - are the historic birthplace of the capital (settled by the Parisii tribe, then the Roman town of Lutetia). En route it passes Troyes and Rouen before reaching the sea.
physical_characteristics: Length 777 km (483 mi), making it France's second-longest river after the Loire. Source elevation approximately 450-471 m on the Langres plateau (commonly cited 447-452 m); mouth at sea level. Drainage basin of about 76,000-79,000 km2 in the Paris Basin, draining roughly one-sixth of metropolitan France and supporting some 17 million people. Average discharge about 310 m3/s in Paris and about 560 m3/s at Le Havre; pluvial oceanic regime with winter highs and summer lows. Known for its many smooth curving loops (boucles); the navigable stretch is heavily channelized, with about 29 weirs and locks between La Basee and Poses, and tidal influence reaching upstream to Poses. The course is conventionally divided into five parts: Petite Seine, Haute Seine, Traverse de Paris, Basse Seine, and Seine maritime (the estuary).
area_or_length: Length: 777 km (483 mi); drainage basin: approximately 76,000-79,000 km2 (about 14% of metropolitan France)
connects_to: Flows into the English Channel (la Manche) via its estuary between Le Havre and Honfleur. Main tributaries: left bank - Yonne, Loing, Eure, Risle; right bank - Ource, Aube, Marne, Oise, Epte (about 45-47 tributaries in total). Via navigation canals it connects to the Loire (Canal de Briare, Canal d'Orleans), the Saone/Rhone (Canal de Bourgogne) and the Scheldt (Oise - Saint-Quentin waterway), linking it to the inland waterway network of northern France and Belgium. Regions crossed: Bourgogne-Franche-Comte, Grand Est, Ile-de-France, Normandy.
role_or_importance: The Seine is France's busiest inland waterway and historically carried most of the country's inland river traffic; it remains a major freight artery (containers, aggregates, grain) serving the ports of Paris, Rouen and Le Havre, and is navigable by ocean-going vessels as far as Rouen, 120 km from the sea. For two millennia it has been the economic lifeline of Paris, supplying water, food, fuel (Morvan timber rafting from 1549), building stone and mill power, and its navigation still appears on the city's coat of arms. Today it shapes the capital's identity, tourism (Bateaux-Mouches cruises, the bouquinistes booksellers), culture (Impressionist iconography) and leisure; after a long swimming ban, cleaned waters hosted the open-water swimming and triathlon events of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games. Politically, Napoleon I named a Paris department after the river, and the City of Paris has owned the source since 1864.
historical_notes: People have settled the Seine valley since prehistoric times; dugout canoes found at Noyen-sur-Seine (ca. 8000 BP) and Bercy in Paris (ca. 5000 BP) attest to very early navigation, and the river has been used as a waterway for some 6,000 years. The Gallic Parisii settled on the Ile de la Cite around the 3rd century BC, and the Romans founded Lutetia there; the river's name derives from Sequana, the Gallo-Roman river goddess worshipped at the source. After Paris became the capital of France in the 12th-13th centuries, the Seine carried grain, wine and timber to the city (stone for Notre-Dame came by boat from the Oise). Vikings sailed longships up the river to sack Paris in 845 and besiege it in 885-886 under Rollo, leading to the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte (911) and the duchy of Normandy. Stone quays appeared in Paris from 1313; timber rafting peaked around 1800; an 1837 law channelized the river for steam navigation; Haussmann's works and the World's Fairs (1855-1937) shaped the modern riverscape; the great 1910 flood drove major flood-protection works. The Banks of the Seine in Paris were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1991, and water-quality efforts since the 1970s (Seine-Aval treatment plant, 2024 Olympics investments) have revived fish populations and public use.
notable_landmarks: In Paris (UNESCO-listed Banks of the Seine between Pont de Sully and Pont d'Iena): Notre-Dame Cathedral and Sainte-Chapelle on the Ile de la Cite, the Louvre, Musee d'Orsay, Eiffel Tower, Grand and Petit Palais, Pont Alexandre III, Pont Neuf (oldest bridge in Paris, 1607), Place de la Concorde, Les Invalides, Palais de Chaillot, the bouquinistes' book stalls and Bateaux-Mouches sightseeing boats. Elsewhere: Rouen's cathedral and old harbors (painted by Monet), the abbey of Jumiages in the lower valley, and the source monument at Source-Seine with a statue of Sequana, property of the City of Paris since 1864.
